facts.fact: Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 at Porbandar, Gujarat.
Gandhi went to South Africa in 1893 for the Dada Abdulla case.
Champaran (1917) was Gandhi's first satyagraha in India.
Kheda (1918) arose because the government refused to remit land revenue despite crop failure.
Gandhi called the Rowlatt Act a 'Black Act'.
General Reginald Dyer ordered the Jallianwala Bagh firing (13 April 1919).
The Dandi March launched the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930.
The Poona Pact (1932) between Gandhi and Ambedkar replaced separate electorates with reserved seats for the Depressed Classes.
Gandhi presided over the Congress only once — Belgaum, 1924.
Gandhi was assassinated on 30 January 1948 by Nathuram Godse.
Gandhi held that pure ends can only be attained through pure means.
Gandhi regarded Gopal Krishna Gokhale as his political guru.
Gandhi's father Karamchand was diwan of Porbandar; his mother was Putlibai.
Gandhi married Kasturba in 1883, at the age of thirteen.
Gandhi studied law at the Inner Temple, London (1888–91), and was called to the bar in 1891.
In June 1893 Gandhi was thrown off a first-class train compartment at Pietermaritzburg.
Gandhi founded the Natal Indian Congress in 1894.
Gandhi started the newspaper Indian Opinion in 1903.
Gandhi raised an Indian Ambulance Corps in the Boer War (1899) and the Zulu (Bambatha) rebellion (1906).
The first satyagraha was resolved at the Empire Theatre, Johannesburg, on 11 September 1906 against the Asiatic registration ordinance (the "Black Act").
Gandhi formed the Passive Resistance Association to defy the registration law; Indians burned their certificates.
The Searle judgment (1913) of the Cape Supreme Court invalidated Hindu, Muslim and Parsi marriages.
A £3 poll tax was levied on ex-indentured Indians who stayed on in Natal.
In November 1913 Gandhi led a march of miners from Newcastle (Natal) into the Transvaal.
The Gandhi–Smuts agreement led to the Indian Relief Act (1914), conceding the main Indian demands.
Gandhi landed at Bombay on 9 January 1915; the date is now Pravasi Bharatiya Divas.
Gandhi set up the Phoenix Settlement near Durban in 1904, inspired by Ruskin's Unto This Last.
Tolstoy Farm (1910) near Johannesburg was set up with Hermann Kallenbach.
In India Gandhi first founded the Satyagraha Ashram at Kochrab, Ahmedabad (1915).
The ashram moved to the banks of the Sabarmati in 1917.
Gandhi settled at Sevagram (Segaon), near Wardha, in 1936.
Ruskin's Unto This Last converted Gandhi to the dignity of labour; he paraphrased it in Gujarati as Sarvodaya.
Tolstoy's The Kingdom of God Is Within You shaped Gandhi's non-violence; the two corresponded.
keys: Kingdom of God Is Within You

facts.fact: Thoreau's essay Civil Disobedience influenced Gandhi.
The Jain thinker Shrimad Rajchandra (Raychandbhai) was a spiritual guide to Gandhi.
Gopal Krishna Gokhale was Gandhi's political guru, who advised him to tour India for a year before taking a public stand.
Gandhi wrote Hind Swaraj in Gujarati in 1909 on board the Kildonan Castle, returning from London to South Africa.
My Experiments with Truth was written in Gujarati (Satyana Prayogo) and serialised in Navajivan from 1925.
Gandhi edited Young India (English weekly) from 1919 to 1932.
Navajivan was Gandhi's Gujarati weekly (from 1919).
Gandhi started the weekly Harijan in February 1933 (with Harijan Bandhu in Gujarati and Harijan Sevak in Hindi).
Gandhi wrote Satyagraha in South Africa in Yerawada jail.
'Songs from Prison' is Gandhi's translation of Indian devotional lyrics.
Gandhi published Constructive Programme: Its Meaning and Place in 1941.
Gandhi also wrote Key to Health and translated the Gita as Anasaktiyoga.
Trusteeship: the rich should hold surplus wealth in trust for society.
Sarvodaya means the welfare (rise) of all.
Gram Swaraj: self-sufficient, self-governing village republics.
Ram Rajya: Gandhi's ideal of a just, moral state.
Nai Talim (Basic Education), the Wardha Scheme of 1937, taught through a productive craft; Zakir Hussain chaired its committee.
Gandhi's 'Talisman' (1947): recall the face of the poorest and weakest man and ask whether your step will help him.
Gandhi listed seven social sins in Young India (1925), such as "politics without principles" and "wealth without work".
The source lists Gandhi's six life-beliefs: truth, non-violence, vegetarianism, brahmacharya, simplicity and faith.
For Gandhi, swadeshi meant serving one's immediate neighbourhood first — economically through khadi and village industry.
Rajkumar Shukla, a Champaran peasant, persuaded Gandhi to come to Champaran (1917).
Under the tinkathia system peasants had to grow indigo on 3 of every 20 kathas of their land.
Synthetic German dyes made indigo unprofitable, so planters demanded higher rents to release peasants.
Gandhi defied an order to leave Champaran and was tried at Motihari.
Gandhi was made a member of the Champaran Agrarian Committee; the Champaran Agrarian Act (1918) ended tinkathia.
Gandhi's Champaran associates included Rajendra Prasad, Mazharul Haq, J.B. Kripalani, Mahadev Desai, Narhari Parikh and Anugrah Narayan Sinha.
At Ahmedabad (1918) the dispute was over withdrawal of the plague bonus; workers asked 50%, owners offered 20%, a tribunal gave 35%.
Anasuya Sarabhai, sister of mill-owner Ambalal Sarabhai, led the workers with Gandhi.
The Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (Majoor Mahajan Sangh) grew out of the strike (1920).
Ahmedabad saw Gandhi's first hunger strike in India.
In Kheda (1918) the revenue code allowed remission if the crop was below 25% of normal.
Patel, Indulal Yagnik and Mohanlal Pandya (the "onion thief") worked with Gandhi in Kheda.
Kheda is called Gandhi's first non-cooperation; Champaran his first civil disobedience.
At the Delhi War Conference (April 1918) Gandhi agreed to recruit Indians for the army — he was called a "recruiting sergeant".
Gandhi campaigned for the end of indentured emigration, which was stopped in 1917.
Gandhi's speech at the opening of Banaras Hindu University (February 1916) attacked the princes' display of wealth.
Gandhi formed the Satyagraha Sabha in Bombay (February 1919) to fight the Rowlatt Bills.
Gandhi was arrested at Palwal on 9 April 1919 while trying to enter Punjab.
Gandhi called his launch of mass satyagraha before people were trained a 'Himalayan miscalculation' (1919).
The Treaty of Sèvres (1920) with Turkey stripped the Caliph of his empire and angered Indian Muslims.
Gandhi presided over the All-India Khilafat Conference at Delhi (November 1919).
Gandhi returned his Kaiser-i-Hind medal (1920) when he launched Non-Cooperation.
Non-Cooperation had three demands — redress of the Punjab wrongs, redress of the Khilafat wrong, and Swaraj.
Gandhi promised 'Swaraj within one year' if the programme was fully carried out.
Gandhi became president of the All India Home Rule League (1920), which he renamed Swarajya Sabha.
In the "Great Trial" (March 1922) Judge Broomfield sentenced Gandhi to six years; he was released in February 1924 on health grounds.
Gandhi fasted for 21 days in September 1924 at Delhi for Hindu–Muslim unity.
Gandhi founded the All India Spinners' Association in 1925.
Gandhi published his Eleven Points in Young India on 31 January 1930 as an ultimatum to Irwin.
Dandi lies on the coast of Navsari district, Gujarat; the march covered about 385 km (240 miles) in 24 days.
Gandhi was arrested at Karadi near Dandi on the night of 4–5 May 1930, before the Dharasana raid.
Tej Bahadur Sapru and M.R. Jayakar mediated between Gandhi and the government in 1930.
Under the Gandhi–Irwin Pact the government withdrew the ordinances and prosecutions and released non-violent prisoners.
The Pact allowed people on the coast to make salt for their own use and permitted peaceful picketing.
The Pact did not grant an inquiry into police excesses nor commute Bhagat Singh's death sentence.
Gandhi sailed to the Second RTC on the SS Rajputana and stayed at Kingsley Hall in London's East End.
Churchill sneered at Gandhi as a 'half-naked fakir' (1931).
Gandhi began his fast against the Communal Award in Yerawada jail on 20 September 1932.
Gandhi founded the All India Anti-Untouchability League in September 1932; it was renamed Harijan Sevak Sangh.
Gandhi made an all-India Harijan tour (November 1933–July 1934).
Gandhi resigned from the Congress in October 1934 to devote himself to constructive work.
Gandhi set up the All India Village Industries Association in 1934.
Gandhi chose Vinoba Bhave as the first individual satyagrahi (October 1940).
Gandhi named Jawaharlal Nehru as his political heir (January 1942).
In the 'Do or Die' speech Gandhi gave instructions for every group — government servants, soldiers, princes, peasants and students.
Gandhi's secretary Mahadev Desai died at the Aga Khan Palace in August 1942.
Kasturba Gandhi died at the Aga Khan Palace on 22 February 1944.
Gandhi was released on health grounds on 6 May 1944 — his last imprisonment.
Subhas Bose first called Gandhi 'Father of the Nation' in a radio broadcast from Singapore on 6 July 1944 (some books say Rangoon).
Gandhi walked through riot-hit Noakhali (East Bengal) from November 1946 to March 1947.
Gandhi's Calcutta fast (September 1947) stopped the riots; Mountbatten called him a 'one-man boundary force'.
On 15 August 1947 Gandhi was in Calcutta, fasting and praying, not at the Delhi celebrations.
Gandhi's last fast (13–18 January 1948, Delhi) was for communal peace and for Pakistan's share of assets (₹55 crore).
Gandhi was shot at Birla House, New Delhi, on 30 January 1948 during his evening prayer.
Nathuram Godse and Narayan Apte were hanged in November 1949 for the murder.
Gandhi's samadhi is at Raj Ghat, Delhi; 30 January is Martyrs' Day.
The UN declared 2 October the International Day of Non-Violence (2007).
Rabindranath Tagore is credited with calling Gandhi 'Mahatma'.
Gandhi called Tagore 'Gurudev'.
Gandhi was affectionately called 'Bapu' (father).
Gandhi called C. Rajagopalachari his 'conscience keeper'.
C.F. Andrews, Gandhi's close friend, was called 'Deenabandhu'.
The AICC met at Bezawada (Vijayawada) on 31 March–1 April 1921 and set the Non-Cooperation targets of ₹1 crore, one crore members and 20 lakh charkhas.
At Bezawada (1921) Pingali Venkayya showed Gandhi a red-and-green flag; a white stripe was added at Gandhi's suggestion and a charkha placed on it.
Gandhi toured Andhra in April–May 1929 to collect funds for khadi.
Gandhi's Harijan tour of 1933–34 included Andhra (December 1933).
The fine hand-spun khadi of Ponduru (Srikakulam) won Gandhi's praise.
Gandhi encouraged the Chirala–Perala satyagraha (1921) of Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya.
In the Salt Satyagraha Bulusu Sambamurthy made salt at Chollangi near Kakinada and was arrested on 18 April 1930.
Champaran Satyagraha — 1917, Bihar (indigo).
Kheda Satyagraha — 1918, Gujarat (land revenue).
The Vaikom Satyagraha (1924–25, Travancore) for the right of avarnas to use temple roads was led by T.K. Madhavan and K.P. Kesava Menon; Gandhi visited in 1925.
The Guruvayur Satyagraha (1931–32) for temple entry was led by K. Kelappan.
Patel led the Borsad Satyagraha (1923–24) in Gujarat against a punitive tax.
The Flag Satyagraha of Nagpur (1923) defended the right to carry the national flag.
Gandhi fasted at Rajkot (March 1939) to press the ruler to honour a promise of reforms.
Gandhi's first fast in India was at Ahmedabad (1918), for the mill-workers.
The 1932 Yerawada fast was against separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.
In May 1933 Gandhi undertook a 21-day self-purification fast for the Harijan cause.
The February 1943 fast at the Aga Khan Palace protested the government blaming the Congress for the 1942 violence.
The September 1947 fast in Calcutta ended the communal riots there.
